versions.rationale: No supported in-scope defect required a content change; unchanged content must not receive a version bump.

findingsReviewed.finding: The skill already distinguishes measured synchronization from incident attribution, includes coordination/scheduling in Reaching, and explains cycle-end timestamps and the Total components.
findingsReviewed.consequence: It avoids blaming the slowest thread exclusively or treating the complete cycle as equal suspension for every thread.
findingsReviewed.disposition: Preserved without changes; do not duplicate the neighboring pause-attribution correction.

findingsReviewed.finding: Ordinary native states, JNI critical regions and FFM critical linkage are separated. critical(false) is explicitly critical, and the checked HotSpot 25 x86 scope is explicit.
findingsReviewed.consequence: A duration label alone does not select a native fix, while blocking work can independently violate the critical option contract.
findingsReviewed.disposition: Confirmed against Java 25 API and tagged OpenJDK source; no new gap.

findingsReviewed.finding: The skill distinguishes JFR event metadata from actual enablement and coverage, joins cycle evidence by identifiers, and treats missing events as incomplete evidence.
findingsReviewed.consequence: Disabled synchronization/end events are not silently interpreted as zero delay or full phase coverage.
findingsReviewed.disposition: Confirmed against the JDK 25 GA profile.jfc; preserved.

findingsReviewed.finding: Actual runtime/build/collector/probe success, conditional loop-poll remediation, and throughput rechecks are already explicit. Failed/obsolete option probes are distinguished from defaults.
findingsReviewed.consequence: Recommendations remain target-specific rather than asserting a portable flag or cost guarantee.
findingsReviewed.disposition: No supported change. Existing historical 25.0.3 observations were not relabeled as freshly executed.

findingsReviewed.finding: JNI collector evolution is separated from the FFM critical option, including G1 region pinning from JDK 22.
findingsReviewed.consequence: Avoids extending old GCLocker behavior to every modern collector/native path.
findingsReviewed.disposition: Fresh primary release-note support confirmed; no edit.

preserved: Focused diagnosis of HotSpot safepoint mechanism, TTSP and non-GC VM operations; neighboring pause/OS/collector ownership remains intact.
Actual-target inspection, successful-probe requirements, collector-specific polling and historically scoped JDK observations.
Timing arithmetic, completed-summary timestamp semantics, operation-versus-synchronization separation and scheduling/coordination caveats.
Native/JNI/FFM distinctions, critical(false) semantics, heap access and lifetime caveats for changing linkage.
JFR configuration, event coverage and correlation limits; timeout warnings are not invented stack samples.
Bounded evidence collection and conditional remediation with throughput/latency checks; no universal tuning recipe.
All four source files, examples, source links, manifest contracts and capability metadata unchanged.
reviewCriteria: Can the agent separate supported timing facts, native-path mechanisms, and unproved causal attribution?
Does it inspect actual binding/options/runtime and change the recommendation when the critical linkage constraint changes?
Does it retain valid ordinary linkage rather than applying a native-duration heuristic?
Does incomplete or disabled instrumentation remain unknown instead of becoming a fabricated zero or thread identity?
Does remediation preserve application/native contracts and avoid unmeasured performance guarantees?

schemaVersion: 1

name: safepoints
version: 1.3.4
description: >-
  The HotSpot safepoint mechanism on JDK 25: thread-local polling words and where the JIT emits polls,
  loop strip mining, global safepoints versus thread-local handshakes, the VM operations
  other than GC that stop the world, time-to-safepoint versus operation time, and reading
  `-Xlog:safepoint`. Use when measured p99 or p99.9 is far worse than the GC log explains,
  when GC logs look clean but latency does not match, when a stop-the-world pause has no GC
  event behind it, when JNI critical regions or runtime/native transitions are suspected, when a
  profiler's hot path never responds to optimisation, or when someone proposes
  `-XX:+UseCountedLoopSafepoints`, `UseThreadLocalHandshakes` or blames `RevokeBias` on a
  modern JDK. Does not cover the introductory TTSP treatment or collector mechanics
  (gc-fundamentals), attributing an observed production pause across GC phase, safepoint and
  OS (pause-attribution), or host-side causes such as CPU throttling and page faults
  (linux-for-jvm).

# TTSP review fixture
This is a synthetic source-and-capture review, not an executed benchmark. The selected production binding and caller are completely represented by the two Java files. The native binary is intentionally absent. Treat the runtime and native contract as supplied facts. All timestamps below use the JVM uptime axis and are aligned within 1 ms. There is no late-thread, native-stack or scheduler capture. The safepoint log contains the completed summary for the one cycle under review. Do not execute the native function or start a JVM.
fixtureFiles.native-contract.md:
# Supplied native function contract
Signature: void await_gate(int budget_ms).
The implementation can block on an internal native mutex for up to budget_ms milliseconds. It does not call Java. There are no pointer arguments, Java-heap addresses or retained Java objects. The library must remain loaded until the call completes. Preserve this native business contract.
fixtureFiles.evidence/safepoint.log: [13.025000s][info][safepoint] Safepoint "ThreadDump", Time since last: 1000000 ns, Reaching safepoint: 24000000 ns, At safepoint: 900000 ns, Leaving safepoint: 100000 ns, Total: 25000000 ns, Threads: 1 / 12
fixtureFiles.ttsp-review.md:
# Proposed diagnosis and fix
Hypothesis: the 80 ms native call blocks every safepoint. Its overlap with the 25 ms cycle proves that it caused TTSP.
Proposed fix: split it into eight native calls.
Preserve JDK 25, G1 and the native business contract.

expected: Write the requested ttsp-review.md artifact, preserving JDK 25/G1 and the native business contract.
Retain the supported timing fact: Reaching is 24 ms of elapsed synchronization, and Total is a 25 ms cycle including At and Leaving; it is not 25 ms of suspension for every thread.
Place the completed cycle approximately at uptime 13.000–13.025 s, within the stated alignment uncertainty; do not start its interval at the completed-summary timestamp.

Separate overlap and the observed high synchronization from proof of a particular late thread or mechanism. Request aligned late-thread/state/native-stack/scheduler evidence as appropriate, rather than inventing it.
Do not edit code or flags, execute native code, attach a profiler, start a JVM, or claim a measured latency improvement.
Inspect the active NativeBinding factory and identify that Linker.Option.critical(false) still requests a critical downcall; false controls heap access and does not disable critical behavior.

Identify a separate, source-supported API contract problem: a potentially 80 ms blocking function does not meet the critical option's all-path short-running constraint, irrespective of whether this capture establishes incident causality.

Recommend removing the critical option for this int-only binding while preserving function signature and library lifetime. Treat it as an API-contract correction, not proof that the incident will be resolved.
Explain that the checked HotSpot 25 x86 critical path can omit the ordinary native-state transition; retain a qualified candidate mechanism without asserting this worker was the late required thread.
failureConditions: Claims overlap alone proves that native-worker caused the 24 ms synchronization delay.
Treats a Java thread-state label as proof of HotSpot safepoint-safe state.
Equates Total with a uniform all-thread stopped interval or treats the summary timestamp as the cycle start.
Applies batching, yield, JVM flags or a collector change as a guaranteed fix without mechanism evidence.
Runs forbidden runtime operations or reports an improvement as measured.
Says critical(false) means critical mode is disabled.
Leaves the blocking function marked critical solely because it has no heap arguments.
Claims reducing an 80 ms call into eight 10 ms calls makes critical usage valid without an all-path constraint.
